MODEL NOTES · VERSION 1

A price informed by other options

This prototype estimates a European equity option using a volatility maturity curve inferred from neighbouring liquid contracts. It is a cross-sectional, market-relative estimate. It does not discover an independent fundamental value or establish that a market price is wrong.

1. Market inputs

Select an equity with listed options, an actual available expiry, a call or put, and a listed strike. The live adapter reads Upstox’s option contracts and chains, then subscribes to its V3 full market feed. The catalogue filters NSE or BSE instruments to equities with unexpired call/put contracts; it does not imply that every listed equity has options. BSE equity-option coverage and liquidity may be limited.

Spot, bids, asks, displayed quantities, open interest and volume come from the provider. The model compares its price with the bid/ask midpoint. Last traded price is shown separately because it may be old. REST timestamps denote retrieval time because that chain response supplies no book timestamp. A feed timestamp indicates the feed message time, not independent proof that an unchanged book was recently refreshed.

The initial live load includes at most six expiries. Streaming subscribes to the underlying, the selected contract and the nearest strikes, up to 1,000 instruments in total. Refresh the chain after a disconnection. Authentication, entitlement and end-to-end streaming require a valid token and have not been verified with an account in this prototype.

The demonstration quotes are generated, not downloaded historical prices. Their date, strikes, premiums and spot are illustrative; they do not establish that a contract actually traded on that date. Imported files are replayed at their own valuation timestamp.

2. A market-based interest-rate curve

The bundled curve uses CCIL’s published Nelson–Siegel–Svensson (NSS) parameters dated 15 October 2026. NSS is a smooth government-bond yield-curve fit. Evaluating it at the option’s exact residual maturity gives a maturity-specific spot yield. A 17.4-day option therefore uses 17.4 days rather than a rounded one-month tenor.

Short-dated NSS outputs are estimates from a fitted bond curve, not observed quotes for a risk-free instrument at every daily maturity. Government-bond rates also need not equal a trader’s funding or collateral curve. The CCIL parameter page does not specify the compounding convention; the app makes the selected convention explicit and marks it unverified. Continuous compounding is the provisional default. Confirm this convention before interpreting small price differences.

T = (expiry timestamp − valuation timestamp) / (365 × 24 hours)
R(T) = continuously compounded zero rate(T) × T
Discount factor D(T) = exp(−R(T))
Forward rate over [a,b] = [R(b) − R(a)] / (b − a)

User-entered curves are interpolated in R(T), equivalently log discount factors. NSS curves are evaluated directly. The simulation uses interval forward rates measured from the valuation date; it does not repeatedly insert a maturity-average zero rate into each time step.

The hosted site ships a dated curve and accepts new JSON curves. Running node server.mjs locally enables the Refresh CCIL button; node scripts/refresh-rates.mjs updates the bundled JSON for the next publication. The hosted site has no automatic daily rate scheduler.

3. Estimate volatility without feeding back the selected price

  1. Remove both the selected option and the opposite call/put at the same strike and expiry. Changing either quote cannot change the fitted price.
  2. Keep two-sided quotes with positive displayed sizes, midpoint-relative spread no greater than 20%, open interest at least 100 in provider units, and traded volume at least 1. Require timestamps within 120 seconds of the snapshot and no more than 5 seconds ahead.
  3. Compute the forward F(T) = spot × exp(R(T) − qT), where q is the assumed continuous dividend yield. Use strikes with |log(K/F)| ≤ 0.08 and the out-of-the-money call or put at each strike.
  4. Invert the European pricing formula using those midpoints, the same rate curve and dividend yield. Reject no-arbitrage-bound violations, IV above 300%, and outliers more than max(5 volatility percentage points, 4 × median absolute deviation) from the expiry median.
  5. Require three distinct strikes per maturity and at least two supported maturities. Form a weighted mean of IV² × T, weighting by 1 / [(0.02 + |log(K/F)|) × (0.02 + relative spread)].
  6. Fit nondecreasing total variance across maturities by weighted isotonic regression, using the number of accepted strikes as node weights. Preserve and display the raw nodes so adjustments can be inspected.
w(T) = maturity volatility(T)² × T
Interval volatility over [a,b] = sqrt([w(b) − w(a)] / (b − a))

Interpolate total variance linearly from (0,0) through the fitted nodes. Interval variance is nonnegative. Before the first node this assumes constant forward variance; beyond the last node pricing is disabled. Daily calculations do not create daily observations: the curve connects the expiries actually supported by market data.

This is a time-only curve around the forward price. It ignores strike-dependent smile/skew and cannot fit every option on the equity. The app flags strikes more than 5% log-moneyness from the forward. Monotone maturity variance does not establish that an entire strike/maturity surface is arbitrage-free. A small spread is also only one liquidity indicator; the fixed thresholds need empirical evaluation.

4. Pricing and Milstein simulation

Under a risk-neutral model, the stock follows dS = (r(t) − q)S dt + σ(t)S dW. The fitted rate and volatility curves are deterministic during a run. The analytical European formula uses integrated R(T), qT and w(T), providing an exact benchmark within these assumptions apart from the numerical normal-CDF approximation.

S(next) = S × [1 + (r − q)Δt + σΔW
                  + ½σ²((ΔW)² − Δt)]
Option estimate = exp(−R(T)) × average terminal payoff

The last term is the Milstein correction. The grid includes all volatility knots and any custom rate knots, with a fractional final step. Antithetic paths use opposite random shocks; the standard error is calculated across independent paired payoff averages. A coupled half-step run uses the same Brownian increments to estimate the time-step effect. Nonpositive paths cause an error instead of being silently clipped.

A default run uses 10,000 paths and a maximum one-calendar-day step. It runs in a browser worker so the interface remains usable. Each run freezes its inputs; live quotes can continue changing separately. The 95% normal sampling interval covers Monte Carlo noise only. It excludes parameter, data, dividend, model and discretisation uncertainty. More paths do not repair an unsuitable volatility curve.

5. What still needs research validation

Daily dividend yields are user assumptions. Known cash dividends, splits, contract adjustments, settlement effects, jumps, stochastic volatility and transaction costs are not modelled. Standard equity-option expiry is assumed to be 15:30 IST; verify any exceptional contract. Prices are quoted per underlying unit; lots and exercise obligations are separate from the displayed theoretical value.

Automated checks cover a known Black–Scholes value, put–call parity, IV inversion, exact expiry time, rate integration, holdout invariance, liquidity rejection, monotone variance, Monte Carlo agreement, pair-based uncertainty and feed decoding. They establish implementation consistency, not accuracy against Indian market prices.

The next empirical study should use timestamped liquid market snapshots, hold each target and its counterpart out, and report errors by expiry and moneyness. Compare against bid/ask spreads, a flat-IV baseline and historical-volatility estimates. Select thresholds on separate data, then evaluate on later untouched snapshots; do not tune on the same observations used for final performance reporting.

Sources & implementation references

  • CCIL: ZCYC parameters and operational aspects. Source usage terms apply to redistribution and commercial use.
  • Upstox Analytics Token, option-chain data, option contracts, instrument files and V3 market feed.
  • QuantLib: BlackVarianceCurve implementation for total-variance interpolation. This app implements its own small engine; it does not use QuantLib.
  • Oxford: Milstein numerical simulation lecture.
  • WebSocket decoding uses protobuf.js 8.8.1, vendored under its BSD licence. The original licence and schema source are included with the source files.
